public_rationale: On 2026-06-15 he wrote that any research you get from AI 'will absolutely have hallucinations.' On a plain reading, every AI research answer contains false or made-up content. A month-long BBC study, reported on 2025-02-11, had journalists review four AI assistants' answers to news questions. They judged that 91% of answers had at least some issue. That leaves about 9% with no issue identified by the reviewers (e1). The same study found that 19% of answers citing BBC content introduced factual errors, such as wrong statements, numbers or dates (e2). A 22-broadcaster study released on 2025-10-22 found major accuracy issues, such as fabricated or outdated information, in 20% of answers (e3). That study counted only major issues, so it does not rule out minor errors in the other answers. These rates show that errors were common. But expert reviewers found no issue in a share of whole answers. That does not fit the claim that every answer contains hallucinations.
limitations: When reviewers found no issue in an answer, that does not prove the answer was error-free. They may have missed subtle errors.
The evaluations used news questions put to general AI assistants. They did not test long or specialised 'deep research' reports, which may be more likely to contain at least one error.
The BBC figures come from a news report about the study, not from the study itself. The 9% and 81% figures are worked out from the reported 91% and 19%.
The 22-broadcaster figures come from one participant's press release.
No source gives an answer-level rate for 2026 models that is specific to hallucinations and includes minor errors.
If the words are read as overstatement for 'expect hallucinations', the high error rates fit that reading better.

our_interpretation: Plain reading: every answer an AI system gives to a research or fact-finding question contains at least one hallucination, meaning false or fabricated content.

Tested with independent evaluations in which expert reviewers checked AI assistants' answers for factual errors. If a meaningful share of answers had no errors, the universal claim is contradicted. High error rates support the speaker's broader warning but not the universal 'any... absolutely'.

No period was given. The claim is read as describing the AI assistants in public use from 2024 up to the post date (2026-06-15). The checking requirement applies to each whole answer, not to single sentences.
criteria.support_condition: Credible evaluations finding that all, or essentially all, AI research answers contain at least one false or fabricated claim.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Credible evaluations finding that a meaningful share of AI answers to research questions contain no factual errors or issues.

evidence.explanation: BBC journalists found that 9% of AI assistant answers had no issues of any kind, so those answers contained no hallucinations. The high issue rate supports the speaker's caution, but not his claim that every answer is affected.

evidence.excerpt: 19% of AI responses which cited BBC content introduced factual errors, for example, incorrect factual statements, numbers and dates.
evidence.explanation: About 81% of AI answers citing BBC content were not found to introduce factual errors. Most answers were not judged to contain fabricated facts.

evidence.excerpt: 45% of all AI answers had at least one significant issue, ranging from incorrect source attribution to factual inaccuracies. Source referencing was especially problematic: in 31% of cases, references were missing or misleading, and 20% of responses contained major accuracy issues such as fabricated or outdated information.
evidence.explanation: In a 22-broadcaster study, 20% of answers had major accuracy issues, so most did not. It counts only major issues, so minor errors in the other answers are not ruled out. It also shows high error rates overall.
